claim: Animals detect motion using a variety of visual cues that reflect regularities in the natural world.
source: Animals detect motion using a variety of visual cues that reflect regularities in the natural world.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research context.

claim: Experiments in animals across phyla have shown that motion percepts incorporate both pairwise and triplet spatiotemporal correlations.
source: Experiments in animals across phyla have shown that motion percepts incorporate both pairwise and triplet spatiotemporal correlations that could theoretically benefit motion computation.
evidence: References prior experimental work across multiple animal species.

claim: Pairwise and triplet spatiotemporal correlations could theoretically benefit motion computation.
source: Experiments in animals across phyla have shown that motion percepts incorporate both pairwise and triplet spatiotemporal correlations that could theoretically benefit motion computation.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on prior work.

claim: Flies combine local pairwise and triplet correlations to reduce variability in motion estimates across natural scenes.
source: Here, we used systematic behavioral measurements of fruit fly motion perception to show how flies combine local pairwise and triplet correlations to reduce variability in motion estimates across natural scenes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on behavioral measurements.

claim: Triplet correlations are useful only when images have light-dark asymmetries that mimic natural ones.
source: By generating synthetic images with statistics controlled by maximum entropy distributions, we show that the triplet correlations are useful only when images have light-dark asymmetries that mimic natural ones.
evidence: This finding is based on experiments with synthetic images.

claim: Asymmetric ON-OFF processing is tuned to the particular statistics of natural scenes.
source: This suggests that asymmetric ON-OFF processing is tuned to the particular statistics of natural scenes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results with synthetic images.

claim: All animals encounter the world's light-dark asymmetries.
source: Since all animals encounter the world's light-dark asymmetries, many visual systems are likely to use asymmetric ON-OFF processing to improve motion estimation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the natural world.

claim: Many visual systems are likely to use asymmetric ON-OFF processing to improve motion estimation.
source: Since all animals encounter the world's light-dark asymmetries, many visual systems are likely to use asymmetric ON-OFF processing to improve motion estimation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings in flies and general principles.

claim: Motion estimation is an important but computationally challenging task for any visual system.
source: For any visual system, motion estimation is an important but computationally challenging task.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Visual systems should take advantage of all useful information to accurately extract motion signals from complex natural inputs.
source: To accurately extract motion signals from complex natural inputs, visual systems should take advantage of all useful information.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle about optimal visual processing.

claim: One source of information for motion estimation lies in the stable statistics of the visual input, that is, in the regularities of natural scenes.
source: One source of information lies in the stable statistics of the visual input, that is, in the regularities of natural scenes (Geisler, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Visual systems are tuned, through evolution and experience, to the statistics of natural environments.
source: A strong version of this hypothesis is that visual systems are tuned, through evolution and experience, to the statistics of natural environments (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Olshausen and Field, 1996; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Srinivasan et al., 1982).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It remains unclear how visual systems use the statistics of natural scenes and the motion signals in them to aid in motion estimation.
source: However, it remains unclear how visual systems use the statistics of natural scenes and the motion signals in them to aid in motion estimation (Salisbury and Palmer, 2016; Sinha et al., 2018).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Motion computation has long been understood algorithmically as selective responses to specific spatiotemporal correlations.
source: Motion computation has long been understood algorithmically as selective responses to specific spatiotemporal correlations (Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Poggio and Reichardt, 1973; Potters and Bialek, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Canonical models propose that animals extract motion from visual signals by detecting pairwise spatiotemporal correlations.
source: For example, canonical models propose that animals extract motion from visual signals by detecting pairwise spatiotemporal correlations (Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956).
evidence: This describes canonical models, supported by citations.

claim: Higher order correlations could also contribute to motion computation.
source: Higher order correlations could also contribute to motion computation, and Bayes optimal visual motion estimators can be written as a sum of terms specialized for detecting different correlation types (Potters and Bialek, 1994; Fitzgerald et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: Bayes optimal visual motion estimators can be written as a sum of terms specialized for detecting different correlation types.
source: Higher order correlations could also contribute to motion computation, and Bayes optimal visual motion estimators can be written as a sum of terms specialized for detecting different correlation types (Potters and Bialek, 1994; Fitzgerald et al., 2011).
evidence: This mathematical result is supported by citations.

claim: This mathematical result follows from a Volterra series expansion.
source: This mathematical result follows from a Volterra series expansion, which provides a general and systematic way to represent nonlinear computational systems.
evidence: This explains the mathematical basis of the result.

claim: Triplet spatiotemporal correlations are the next lowest-order terms after pairwise correlations.
source: For example, triplet spatiotemporal correlations are the next lowest-order terms after pairwise correlations, and both humans and flies perceive motion in 'glider' stimuli that isolate triplet spatiotemporal correlations (Clark et al., 2014; Hu and Victor, 2010).
evidence: This is a mathematical fact about the Volterra series.

claim: Both humans and flies perceive motion in 'glider' stimuli that isolate triplet spatiotemporal correlations.
source: For example, triplet spatiotemporal correlations are the next lowest-order terms after pairwise correlations, and both humans and flies perceive motion in 'glider' stimuli that isolate triplet spatiotemporal correlations (Clark et al., 2014; Hu and Victor, 2010).
evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations.

claim: The sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations shows that motion perception incorporates cues neglected by canonical motion detectors.
source: The sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations shows that motion perception incorporates cues neglected by canonical motion detectors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the empirical findings.

claim: Perceptual sensitivities to triplet spatiotemporal correlations prove that visual systems must consider the polarity of contrast when computing motion.
source: Interestingly, perceptual sensitivities to triplet spatiotemporal correlations prove that visual systems must consider the polarity of contrast when computing motion.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the properties of triplet correlations.

claim: Triplet correlations flip sign when contrast polarities are inverted.
source: This is because triplet correlations flip sign when contrast polarities are inverted, which means that the perceptual contribution of triplet correlations to a motion estimator reverses when all input contrasts are inverted.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of triplet correlations.

claim: The perceptual contribution of triplet correlations to a motion estimator reverses when all input contrasts are inverted.
source: This is because triplet correlations flip sign when contrast polarities are inverted, which means that the perceptual contribution of triplet correlations to a motion estimator reverses when all input contrasts are inverted.
evidence: This follows logically from the sign-flipping property.

claim: Contrast-polarity dependent motion processing has been hypothesized to be an adaptation to natural scenes, especially to the light-dark asymmetry of the contrast distribution.
source: This contrast-polarity dependent motion processing has been hypothesized to be an adaptation to natural scenes, especially to the light-dark asymmetry of the contrast distribution (Clark et al., 2014; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Leonhardt et al., 2016; Nitzany and Victor, 2014).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Simulated motion detectors that were optimized to estimate motion in natural scenes exhibited contrast-polarity-dependent responses similar to flies.
source: For example, simulated motion detectors that were optimized to estimate motion in natural scenes exhibited contrast-polarity-dependent responses similar to flies (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Leonhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from modeling studies, supported by citations.

claim: Modeling studies suggest that contrast-polarity-dependent responses emerge from performance optimization in natural scenes.
source: These modeling studies suggest that contrast-polarity-dependent responses emerge from performance optimization in natural scenes, but they do not show that real visual systems use their sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations to improve motion estimates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of modeling studies.

claim: Previous modeling studies do not show that real visual systems use their sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations to improve motion estimates.
source: These modeling studies suggest that contrast-polarity-dependent responses emerge from performance optimization in natural scenes, but they do not show that real visual systems use their sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations to improve motion estimates.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of prior work.

claim: Previous experimental studies measured sensitivities to only a few triplet correlations.
source: This limitation arises because previous experimental studies measured sensitivities to only a few triplet correlations (Clark et al., 2014; Leonhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a limitation of prior experimental work, supported by citations.

claim: One cannot assess the utility of individual correlations in isolation.
source: However, one cannot assess the utility of individual correlations in isolation (Clark et al., 2014; Nitzany et al., 2016), and naturalistic visual signals contain many spatiotemporal correlations with diverse spatiotemporal structures.
evidence: This is a methodological principle supported by citations.

claim: Naturalistic visual signals contain many spatiotemporal correlations with diverse spatiotemporal structures.
source: However, one cannot assess the utility of individual correlations in isolation (Clark et al., 2014; Nitzany et al., 2016), and naturalistic visual signals contain many spatiotemporal correlations with diverse spatiotemporal structures.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural visual signals.

claim: Previous analyses recognized that some kind of light-dark asymmetry is required for triplet correlation sensitivity to emerge in optimized motion estimators.
source: Moreover, although previous analyses recognized that some kind of light-dark asymmetry is required for triplet correlation sensitivity to emerge in optimized motion estimators (Clark et al., 2014; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Leonhardt et al., 2016), they did not discover which statistical regularities within natural scenes were sufficient for the observed motion signals to improve accuracy.
evidence: This describes findings from prior analyses, supported by citations.

claim: Previous analyses did not discover which statistical regularities within natural scenes were sufficient for the observed motion signals to improve accuracy.
source: Moreover, although previous analyses recognized that some kind of light-dark asymmetry is required for triplet correlation sensitivity to emerge in optimized motion estimators (Clark et al., 2014; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Leonhardt et al., 2016), they did not discover which statistical regularities within natural scenes were sufficient for the observed motion signals to improve accuracy.
evidence: This identifies a gap in prior work.

claim: The study systematically measured the nonlinearities in Drosophila visual motion detection and related them to light-dark asymmetries in natural scenes.
source: Here, we filled these gaps by systematically measuring the nonlinearities in Drosophila visual motion detection and relating them to light-dark asymmetries in natural scenes.
evidence: This describes the overall approach of the study.

claim: The study characterized low-order components of the fly's motion computation algorithm by modeling its visually evoked turning behavior with a Volterra series expansion.
source: We first systematically characterized low-order components of the fly's motion computation algorithm by modeling its visually evoked turning behavior with a Volterra series expansion (Clark et al., 2011; Clark et al., 2014; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Marmarelis and McCann, 1973; Poggio and Reichardt, 1973; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology, supported by citations to prior use of this approach.

claim: The study extended canonical pairwise (second-order) motion computation models by adding a triplet (third-order) component that accounts for contrast-polarity-dependent motion computation.
source: Through this framework, we extended canonical pairwise (second-order) motion computation models by adding a triplet (third-order) component that accounts for contrast-polarity-dependent motion computation.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The study evaluated the performance of the inferred algorithm across an ensemble of moving natural images.
source: We evaluated the performance of the inferred algorithm across an ensemble of moving natural images and discovered that the third-order component improves velocity estimates by canceling image-induced variability in the second-order component.
evidence: This describes the evaluation methodology.

claim: The third-order component improves velocity estimates by canceling image-induced variability in the second-order component.
source: We evaluated the performance of the inferred algorithm across an ensemble of moving natural images and discovered that the third-order component improves velocity estimates by canceling image-induced variability in the second-order component.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: The study leveraged maximum entropy distributions to develop a method for generating synthetic images with precisely controlled contrast statistics.
source: Finally, we leveraged maximum entropy distributions to develop a method for generating synthetic images with precisely controlled contrast statistics.
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation of the study.

claim: The skewness of natural images allows the fly's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations to improve its canonical motion estimates.
source: This method revealed that the skewness of natural images allows the fly's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations to improve its canonical motion estimates.
evidence: This is a key finding from the synthetic image experiments.

claim: The HRC exemplifies canonical motion detectors, which rely exclusively on pairwise spatiotemporal correlations to estimate motion.
source: The HRC exemplifies canonical motion detectors, which rely exclusively on pairwise spatiotemporal correlations to estimate motion (Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the HRC model, supported by citations and Figure 1A.

claim: The HRC can be equivalently written as a motion energy model.
source: It can be equivalently written as a motion energy model (Adelson and Bergen, 1985).
evidence: This is a known equivalence in the field, supported by citation.

claim: The study used a database of natural, panoramic photographs to create naturalistic motion stimuli.
source: We used a database of natural, panoramic photographs to create naturalistic motion stimuli (Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the data source, supported by citation.

claim: The study converted the photographs' luminance signals into local contrast signals.
source: In particular, we first converted the photographs' luminance signals into local contrast signals (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step, illustrated in figures.

claim: The study rigidly translated natural images at various horizontal velocities to simulate full-field motion signals.
source: We then rigidly translated these natural images at various horizontal velocities to simulate full-field motion signals (Badwan et al., 2019; Dror et al., 2001; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Leonhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation method, supported by citations.

claim: Rigid translation of images mimics the motion produced by an animal's pure rotation.
source: This rigid translation of images mimics the motion produced by an animal's pure rotation, during which visual objects all move at the same rotational velocity and occlusion does not change over time.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the stimulus choice.

claim: Real motion through an environment generates more complex signals than rigid translations.
source: Real motion through an environment generates more complex signals than this, but rigid translations are straightforward to compute and rotational visual stimuli are known to induce the rotational optomotor response that we focus on in this manuscript.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the stimulus approach.

claim: Rotational visual stimuli are known to induce the rotational optomotor response.
source: Real motion through an environment generates more complex signals than this, but rigid translations are straightforward to compute and rotational visual stimuli are known to induce the rotational optomotor response that we focus on in this manuscript.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly behavior.

claim: The HRC model generated a mean response that was linearly tuned for small velocities, peaked at around 130 °/s, and then decayed to zero for fast speeds.
source: The model generated a mean response that was linearly tuned for small velocities, peaked at around 130 °/s, and then decayed to zero for fast speeds (Figure 1C green line).
evidence: This is a result from simulations, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Substantial variance was observed about the mean HRC response to natural scenes.
source: However, we observed substantial variance about the mean response, and this variance implies that different natural scenes generated different second-order motion estimates, even when moving at the same velocity (Figure 1C green shading).
evidence: This is an observation from simulations, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Different natural scenes generated different second-order motion estimates, even when moving at the same velocity.
source: However, we observed substantial variance about the mean response, and this variance implies that different natural scenes generated different second-order motion estimates, even when moving at the same velocity (Figure 1C green shading).
evidence: This is an inference from the observed variance.

claim: Canonical second-order motion detectors generate variable responses with natural scene inputs.
source: This is consistent with the finding that canonical second-order motion detectors generate variable responses with natural scene inputs (Dror et al., 2001; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Sinha et al., 2018).
evidence: This finding is consistent with prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The study generated a synthetic image set in which the second-order statistics of natural scenes were preserved, but all higher order structure was eliminated.
source: To demonstrate this, we generated a synthetic image set in which we preserved the second-order statistics of natural scenes, including their spatial correlation function and contrast variance, but eliminated all higher order structure (Figure 1D, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: When the higher order structure was eliminated, the HRC's average tuning was unchanged, but there was a marked decrease in the variance.
source: When the higher order structure was eliminated, the HRC's average tuning was unchanged, but there was a marked decrease in the variance (Figure 1C purple).
evidence: This is a result from simulations with synthetic images, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Higher order structure in natural scenes induces variability in canonical motion estimates.
source: This demonstrates that higher order structure in natural scenes induces variability in canonical motion estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of natural and synthetic images.

claim: Motion computation requires a nonlinear transformation to form a motion estimate from the visual stimulus.
source: Motion computation requires a nonlinear transformation to form a motion estimate from the visual stimulus (Borst and Egelhaaf, 1989; Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Poggio and Reichardt, 1973).
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The study approximated the nonlinear transformation of motion computation using a Volterra series expansion.
source: We approximated this nonlinear transformation using a Volterra series expansion (Marmarelis and McCann, 1973; Marmarelis, 2004; Schetzen, 1980; Wiener, 1966).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach, supported by citations.

claim: The Volterra series is a polynomial description of a nonlinearity, with a first-order kernel that describes linear transformations, a second-order kernel that captures quadratic terms, and higher-order kernels that combine to represent a wide variety of nonlinearities beyond the second-order.
source: Similar to the Taylor series from calculus, the Volterra series is a polynomial description of a nonlinearity, with a first-order kernel that describes linear transformations, a second-order kernel that captures quadratic terms, and higher-order kernels that combine to represent a wide variety of nonlinearities beyond the second-order.
evidence: This explains the mathematical properties of the Volterra series.

claim: Many polynomial terms can be needed to describe some nonlinearities.
source: However, many polynomial terms can be needed to describe some nonlinearities.
evidence: This is a limitation of polynomial approximations.

claim: The polynomial description of a compressive, saturating nonlinearity is inefficient.
source: For instance, the polynomial description of a compressive, saturating nonlinearity is inefficient, and it can be easier to describe such transformations using alternative nonlinear model architectures, such as linear-nonlinear cascade models (Dayan and Abbott, 2001).
evidence: This is a known limitation of polynomial approximations, supported by citation.

claim: The Volterra kernel description is explicitly algorithmic.
source: We emphasize that the Volterra kernel description is explicitly algorithmic, as it aims to summarize the overall system processing without considering the mechanisms leading to this processing.
evidence: This clarifies the level of description provided by Volterra kernels.

claim: Volterra kernels allow us to rigorously group response properties by their order.
source: Volterra kernels are useful for studying visual motion processing because they allow us to rigorously group response properties by their order (Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Potters and Bialek, 1994), thereby permitting us to clearly describe both canonical and contrast polarity-dependent components of the behavior.
evidence: This explains the utility of Volterra kernels, supported by citations.

claim: The second-order kernel is equivalent to the canonical motion detecting algorithms, as it explains the sensitivity to pairwise spatiotemporal correlations.
source: For example, the second-order kernel is equivalent to the canonical motion detecting algorithms, as it explains the sensitivity to pairwise spatiotemporal correlations (Fitzgerald et al., 2011; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an established equivalence, supported by citations.

claim: Second-order Volterra kernels have been used to model second-order behavior and neural processing in flies and primates.
source: Second-order Volterra kernels, along with related spike-triggered covariance methods (Bialek and van Steveninck, 2005; Sandler and Marmarelis, 2015; Schwartz et al., 2006), have been used to model second-order behavior and neural processing in flies and primates (Clark et al., 2011; Marmarelis and McCann, 1973; Poggio and Reichardt, 1973; Rust et al., 2005; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes prior applications of the method, supported by citations.

claim: The second-order kernel cannot capture the system's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations.
source: However, the second-order kernel cannot capture the system's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations.
evidence: This is a mathematical limitation of second-order kernels.

claim: The third-order kernel directly measures sensitivities to triplet spatiotemporal correlations and probes ON/OFF asymmetries in motion processing.
source: The third-order kernel directly measures sensitivities to triplet spatiotemporal correlations and probes ON/OFF asymmetries in motion processing.
evidence: This explains what the third-order kernel captures.

claim: The study focused on how the fly responds to correlations between nearest-neighbor pixels in the visual input.
source: We focused on how the fly responds to correlations between nearest-neighbor pixels in the visual input, which corresponded roughly to a single ommatidium separation (Buchner, 1976) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the spatial scale of the analysis, supported by citation and Figure 2A.

claim: The second-order kernel describes how the behavioral response is influenced by the product of contrasts at each pair of spatiotemporal points in the visual input.
source: The second-order kernel describes how the behavioral response is influenced by the product of contrasts at each pair of spatiotemporal points in the visual input (Figure 2B blue).
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the second-order kernel, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The third-order kernel describes how the response is influenced by the product of contrasts at each triplet of spatiotemporal points in the visual input.
source: In comparison, the third-order kernel describes how the response is influenced by the product of contrasts at each triplet of spatiotemporal points in the visual input (Figure 2B green).
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the third-order kernel, illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Triplet spatiotemporal correlations could in principle be computed across three distinct spatial locations.
source: Note that triplet spatiotemporal correlations could in principle be computed across three distinct spatial locations, but our analysis focused on triplet spatiotemporal correlations distributed across two nearest-neighbor pixels.
evidence: This clarifies the scope of the analysis.

claim: The study developed a high-throughput setup to measure turning in walking flies in response to visual stimuli.
source: In order to extract Volterra kernels, especially higher-order ones, we needed a large amount of data. We thus developed a high-throughput setup to measure turning in walking flies in response to visual stimuli (Figure 2C) (Creamer et al., 2018; Creamer et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup, supported by citations and Figure 2C.

claim: A fly's optomotor turning response serves as a readout of its motion perception.
source: In this setup, a fly's optomotor turning response serves as a readout of its motion perception (Götz and Wenking, 1973; Hassenstein and Reichardt, 1956), which allowed us to characterize the fly's motion computation algorithm by measuring its visually-evoked turning response.
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Flies spend a large portion of their lives standing and walking on surfaces, making walking optomotor responses ethologically critical.
source: Flies spend a large portion of their lives standing and walking on surfaces, making walking optomotor responses ethologically critical (Carey et al., 2006).
evidence: This justifies the choice of behavioral assay, supported by citation.

claim: The study extracted the second- and third-order Volterra-kernels with reverse-correlation methods.
source: We extracted the second- and third-order Volterra-kernels with reverse-correlation methods.
evidence: This describes the analysis method.

claim: The study presented flies with spatiotemporally uncorrelated binary stimuli on a panoramic screen around the fly, measured their turning responses, and correlated the behavior at each time to the stimuli preceding it.
source: To do this, we presented flies with spatiotemporally uncorrelated binary stimuli on a panoramic screen around the fly, measured their turning responses, and correlated the behavior at each time to the stimuli preceding it (Materials and methods, Appendix 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Clark et al., 2011; Mano and Clark, 2017; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, supported by citations and supplementary figures.

claim: The measured second-order kernel showed positive and negative lobes.
source: The measured second-order kernel showed positive and negative lobes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The positive lobe below the diagonal in the second-order kernel indicates that flies turned to the right when presented with positive correlations in the rightward direction.
source: The positive lobe below the diagonal indicates that flies turned to the right when presented with positive correlations in the rightward direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kernel structure.

claim: The measured second-order kernel is consistent with classical models of motion computation and with previous neural and behavioral measurements.
source: This second-order kernel is consistent with classical models of motion computation and with previous neural and behavioral measurements (Clark et al., 2011; Marmarelis and McCann, 1973; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016).
evidence: This compares the results to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The measured third-order kernel showed both positive and negative values.
source: The measured third-order kernel also showed both positive and negative values (Figure 2E), and we will dissect its detailed structure later in this manuscript.
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The output of the model to moving visual stimuli is the predicted optomotor turning response.
source: The kernels were fit to turning behavior, so the output of the model to moving visual stimuli is the predicted optomotor turning response.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the model output.

claim: Optomotor turning responses provide a proxy for the fly's velocity estimate.
source: Following previous work (Clark et al., 2014; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Leonhardt et al., 2016; Poggio and Reichardt, 1973; Potters and Bialek, 1994; Sinha et al., 2018), we hypothesized that optomotor turning responses provide a proxy for the fly's velocity estimate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The study evaluated the fly's motion computation performance with the metric of how accurately the behavioral algorithm predicts the image velocity when an entire natural image translates rigidly with constant velocity.
source: Using the fitted behavioral model, we could thus investigate how accurately the fly's velocity estimate tracks the true image velocity. We evaluated the fly's motion computation performance with a simple and specific metric: when an entire natural image translates rigidly with constant velocity, how accurately does the behavioral algorithm predict the image velocity (Figure 3A)?
evidence: This describes the evaluation approach, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The study sampled velocities from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution with a standard deviation of 114 °/s.
source: We sampled the velocities from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution with a standard deviation of 114 °/s: this distribution roughly matched turning distributions in walking flies (DeAngelis et al., 2019; Katsov and Clandinin, 2008).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters, justified by citations.

claim: The second-order response describes how the fly responded to naturalistic second-order spatiotemporal correlations in the stimulus.
source: The second-order response is the output from the second-order kernel, and it describes how the fly responded to naturalistic second-order spatiotemporal correlations in the stimulus.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the second-order response.

claim: The study quantified how well the model's responses predicted the image velocity using the Pearson correlation coefficient.
source: We quantified how well the model's responses predicted the image velocity using the Pearson correlation coefficient (Clark et al., 2014; Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Leonhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the evaluation metric, supported by citations.

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficient metric supposes that the model response and image velocity are linearly related.
source: This metric supposes that the model response and image velocity are linearly related, and its value summarizes intuitively the mean-squared-error of the best linear fit between the model's output and the image velocity.
evidence: This explains the properties of the metric.

claim: When the correlation coefficient has an absolute value near 1, the model closely tracks image velocity.
source: When the correlation coefficient has an absolute value near 1, the model closely tracks image velocity, while a value near 0 indicates no linear relationship between model and image velocity.
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the metric.

claim: The fly's third-order response on its own would predict that the fly turns in the direction opposite to the presented motion.
source: This means that the fly's third-order response on its own would predict that the fly turns in the direction opposite to the presented motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the anti-correlation result.

claim: The third-order responses improve velocity estimates only in conjunction with second-order responses.
source: This important result shows that the third-order responses improve velocity estimates only in conjunction with second-order responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: The second-order response is influenced by both the image velocity and the structure of the natural scene.
source: To understand this counterintuitive finding, it's useful to recognize that the second-order response is influenced by both the image velocity and the structure of the natural scene.
evidence: This is an interpretation to explain the results.

claim: The output of the HRC depended both on the velocity of motion and on the particular image that was moving.
source: For example, recall that the output of the HRC depended both on the velocity of motion and on the particular image that was moving (Figure 1C).
evidence: This refers back to an earlier result, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: One way to improve the accuracy of the response is to reduce scene-dependent variability in the second-order estimate.
source: Thus, one way to improve the accuracy of the response is to reduce scene-dependent variability in the second-order estimate.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how to improve performance.

claim: The third-order signal was strongly anticorrelated with the scene-induced residual in the second-order response.
source: To investigate whether this interpretation explained the observed improvement, we calculated the residuals of the second-order responses by subtracting the best linear fit of the image velocity and plotted them against the third-order responses. We found that the third-order signal was strongly anticorrelated with this scene-induced residual in the second-order response (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The fly's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations canceled scene-dependent variability in the second-order motion estimator to improve the accuracy of motion estimation across natural scenes.
source: This means that the fly's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations indeed canceled scene-dependent variability in the second-order motion estimator to improve the accuracy of motion estimation across natural scenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the residual analysis.

claim: The measured second- and third-order kernels were weighted near optimally for performance in naturalistic motion estimation.
source: Thus, the measured second- and third-order kernels were weighted near optimally for performance in naturalistic motion estimation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optimization analysis.

claim: The improvement added by the third-order response did not depend strongly on the variance of the velocity.
source: To see how it depended on the width of the image velocity distribution, we varied the standard deviation over an order of magnitude. The improvement did not depend strongly on the variance of the velocity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from parameter sweeps, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When local contrasts were computed on a length scale of 25°, this approximates the spatial scale of surround inhibition measured in flies.
source: When we previously converted luminance into contrast signals, we computed local contrasts on a length scale of 25° (measured by full-width-at-half-maximum), because that is the approximate spatial scale of surround inhibition measured in flies (Arenz et al., 2017; Freifeld et al., 2013; Srinivasan et al., 1982).
evidence: This justifies a parameter choice, supported by citations.

claim: When the spatial scale of contrast computation was swept from 10° to 75°, the improvement added by the third-order kernel first increased, peaked at around 30°, and then decreased to negative values after 40°.
source: When we swept this spatial scale from 10° to 75°, the improvement added by the third-order kernel first increased, peaked at around 30°, and then decreased to negative values after 40° (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is a result from parameter sweeps, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: When contrasts were computed over time instead of space, improvements were observed on timescales less than 100 ms, comparable to measured timescales involved in early visual neurons that compute temporal derivatives.
source: When we computed the contrast over time, instead of space, we observed improvements on timescales less than 100 ms, comparable to measured timescales involved in early visual neurons that compute temporal derivatives (Behnia et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 1982; Yang et al., 2016) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2FG).
evidence: This is a result from parameter sweeps, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and compared to prior work.

claim: The third-order term hurt performance when contrasts were computed on longer timescales.
source: However, the third-order term hurt performance when contrasts were computed on longer timescales.
evidence: This is a result from parameter sweeps.

claim: Contrast computations influence the utility of the measured third-order kernel, with maximal utility occurring in a regime that approximately matches the contrast computation of the fly eye.
source: These results show that contrast computations influence the utility of the measured third-order kernel, with maximal utility occurring in a regime that approximately matches the contrast computation of the fly eye.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the parameter sweep results.

claim: The impulse response of a system is its output when presented with a small and brief input, called an impulse.
source: The impulse response of a system is its output when presented with a small and brief input, called an impulse.
evidence: This is a definition from systems theory.

claim: If the impulse consists of a contrast triplet over three points in space and time, then the triplet impulse response captures the system's response to the interactions of those three points, after accounting for those responses already explained by linear or second-order impulse responses.
source: Analogously, if the impulse consists of a contrast triplet over three points in space and time, then the triplet impulse response captures the system's response to the interactions of those three points, after accounting for those responses already explained by linear or second-order impulse responses.
evidence: This extends the impulse response concept to third-order.

claim: The kernel predicts that the behavioral consequences of triplet correlations will last almost a second.
source: The predicted time course of the behavioral effect is easy to discern, and the kernel predicts that the behavioral consequences of triplet correlations will last almost a second.
evidence: This is an observation from the kernel visualization.

claim: The impact of different triplet correlations varies significantly in both direction and magnitude.
source: As expected, the impact of different triplet correlations varies significantly in both direction and magnitude.
evidence: This is an observation from the kernel analysis.

claim: The study verified the reliability of the third-order kernel measurement by extracting an ensemble of null kernels by applying the reverse-correlation analysis to the measured behavioral responses and temporally-shifted visual stimuli.
source: We verified the reliability of our third-order kernel measurement in two ways. First, we tested the statistical significance of the measured kernel directly. We extracted an ensemble of null kernels by applying the reverse-correlation analysis to the measured behavioral responses and temporally-shifted visual stimuli (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a validation method.

claim: Many terms in the third-order kernel were statistically significant at the p=0.05 level.
source: By comparing summed kernel elements in the empirical and null kernels, we found that many terms in the third-order kernel were statistically significant at the p=0.05 level (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from statistical testing, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Significance was especially common when the temporal distance between the points in the triplet spatiotemporal correlation was less than 0.1 s.
source: Significance was especially common when the temporal distance between the points in the triplet spatiotemporal correlation was less than 0.1 s.
evidence: This is an observation from the statistical testing.

claim: The study measured the fly's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations with third-order glider stimuli.
source: Second, we measured the fly's sensitivity to triplet spatiotemporal correlations with third-order glider stimuli (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a validation experiment, illustrated in figures.

claim: Third-order glider stimuli are binary stimuli that lack pairwise correlations and are enriched in specific triplet spatiotemporal correlations.
source: Third-order glider stimuli are binary stimuli that lack pairwise correlations and are enriched in specific triplet spatiotemporal correlations (Clark et al., 2014; Hu and Victor, 2010).
evidence: This defines glider stimuli, supported by citations.

claim: The study used the measured third-order kernel to predict responses to the glider stimuli.
source: We used the measured third-order kernel to predict responses to the glider stimuli.
evidence: This describes the validation approach.

claim: Most of the measured responses to glider stimuli were quantitatively predicted by the third-order kernel.
source: Most of the measured responses were quantitatively predicted by the third-order kernel (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a result from the validation experiment, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Several gliders elicited smaller behavioral responses compared to the kernel prediction.
source: Several gliders elicited smaller behavioral responses compared to the kernel prediction; such differences might be attributable to induced long-range spatial correlations in glider stimuli (Clark et al., 2014; Hu and Victor, 2010), which are not captured by our measured nearest-neighbor kernel.
evidence: This is an observation from the validation experiment, with a possible explanation supported by citations.

claim: The successes revealed by the independent experimental test strongly suggest that there was enough statistical power to reliably fit the third-order kernel to the behavioral data.
source: Nevertheless, the successes revealed by this independent experimental test strongly suggest that we had enough statistical power to reliably fit the third-order kernel to the behavioral data.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results.

claim: Multiple models propose that sensitivity to pairwise and triplet spatiotemporal correlations could emerge simultaneously from the same nonlinear step in the fly brain.
source: Multiple models propose that sensitivity to pairwise and triplet spatiotemporal correlations could emerge simultaneously from the same nonlinear step in the fly brain (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Leong et al., 2016; Leonhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes prior modeling work, supported by citations.

claim: The summed kernel strengths showed that the second-order and third-order kernels had similar sensitivities to temporal delays between the input pixels, with peak sensitivity at the shortest delays in the experiment.
source: The summed kernel strengths showed that the second-order and third-order kernels had similar sensitivities to temporal delays between the input pixels, with peak sensitivity at the shortest delays in our experiment (Figure 4E bottom).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the kernels, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: An analysis employing the singular value decomposition yielded similar results and also showed comparable kinetics in the behavioral responses to pairwise and triplet correlations.
source: An analysis employing the singular value decomposition yielded similar results, and also showed comparable kinetics in the behavioral responses to pairwise and triplet correlations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2EFG).
evidence: This is a result from an alternative analysis, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A recent theoretical study proposed several motion detectors whose parameters were optimized for velocity estimation in natural scenes.
source: A recent theoretical study proposed several motion detectors whose parameters were optimized for velocity estimation in natural scenes (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes prior theoretical work, supported by citation and supplementary figure.

claim: The third-order kernels of the optimized models were usually similar to each other.
source: We found that the third-order kernels of the optimized models were usually similar to each other (Figure 4F), which is consistent with prior analyses (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015).
evidence: This is a result from comparing optimized models, shown in Figure 4F and consistent with prior work.

claim: The measured third-order kernel consistently agreed with the optimized kernels in its signs.
source: The measured third-order kernel consistently agreed with the optimized kernels in its signs, and in some cases, the kernels were also similar in magnitude.
evidence: This is a result from comparing measured and optimized kernels.

claim: Certain kernel elements differed markedly between the optimized models and the behaviorally measured kernel.
source: However, certain kernel elements differed markedly between the optimized models and the behaviorally measured kernel.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison.

claim: The behavioral kernel was much smaller than the optimized kernels for correlations whose spatiotemporal structure involved large delays between the points.
source: Perhaps most noticeably, the behavioral kernel was much smaller than the optimized kernels for correlations whose spatiotemporal structure involved large delays between the points (Figure 4F, third and fifth kernel elements).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Differences between the optimized models and the measured behavior could indicate suboptimalities in the fly brain.
source: Such differences between the optimized models and the measured behavior could indicate suboptimalities in the fly brain.
evidence: This is one possible interpretation of the differences.

claim: Differences between optimized models and measured behavior could also result from unrealistic constraints imposed on the model optimization.
source: However, they could also result from unrealistic constraints imposed on the model optimization, such as fixed temporal processing and restricted model structures (Fitzgerald and Clark, 2015; Leonhardt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: The measured kernel provides valuable new data to inform theoretical work assessing the optimality of biological motion estimators.
source: The measured kernel therefore provides valuable new data to inform theoretical work assessing the optimality of biological motion estimators.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the value of the measurements.

claim: The natural scene dataset is comprised of heterogeneous individual images.
source: The natural scene dataset is comprised of heterogeneous individual images (Figure 5A), so we calculated the contrast mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis of each image individually.
evidence: This describes the dataset, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: Each of the statistics (variance, skewness, kurtosis) showed a wide distribution over the image ensemble.
source: Each of these statistics showed a wide distribution over the image ensemble (Figure 5—figure supplement 1ABCD).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Image statistics were highly dependent on each other: a positively skewed image often had high variance and was highly kurtotic.
source: These statistics were also highly dependent on each other: a positively skewed image often had high variance and was highly kurtotic (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in figures.

claim: Strong relationships between image statistics make it difficult to isolate the effects of individual statistics within the image ensemble.
source: These strong relationships make it difficult to isolate the effects of individual statistics within the image ensemble.
evidence: This is a methodological challenge identified from the data.

claim: The study generated several different synthetic image datasets that have alternate contrast statistics to isolate the effects of individual statistics.
source: To isolate the effects of individual statistics, we therefore generated several different synthetic image datasets that have alternate contrast statistics (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the methodological solution.

claim: The study constructed a synthetic contrast distribution and sampled pixel contrasts from this distribution to generate each image.
source: To generate each image, we constructed a synthetic contrast distribution and sampled pixel contrasts from this distribution (Appendix 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This describes the image generation method, illustrated in supplementary figures.

claim: The study manipulated the statistics of the image by constraining various statistics of the distribution.
source: In this way, we could manipulate the statistics of the image by constraining various statistics of the distribution.
evidence: This explains the approach for controlling image statistics.

claim: The study constrained the distribution to have specific lower order moments, such as mean, variance, and skewness.
source: In particular, we constrained the distribution to have specific lower order moments, such as mean, variance, and skewness.
evidence: This describes the specific constraints used.

claim: A distribution is not solely determined by its lower order moments, so there can be many distributions sharing the same lower order moments.
source: A distribution is not solely determined by its lower order moments, so there can be many distributions sharing the same lower order moments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a mathematical fact, illustrated in supplementary figures.

claim: Among all distributions sharing the same lower order moments, the study chose the most random one, known as the maximum entropy distribution (MED).
source: Among all such distributions, we chose the most random one, known as the maximum entropy distribution (MED) (Berger et al., 1996; Jaynes, 1957; Schneidman et al., 2006; Victor and Conte, 2012).
evidence: This describes the method for selecting the distribution, supported by citations.

claim: The study generated two synthetic image datasets: one with the same contrast mean and variance as natural images, and another with the same mean, variance, and skewness.
source: We began by generating two synthetic image datasets (Materials and methods). In the first dataset, we generated a synthetic image for each natural image that had the same contrast mean and variance. To do this, we first found an MED whose contrast mean and variance matched those of the natural image (Figure 5C, green). We then generated a single synthetic image by sampling from this MED (Figure 5D green). In the second dataset, we required the synthetic image to have the same contrast mean, variance, and skewness as the original image (Figure 5CD, brown).
evidence: This describes the synthetic datasets, illustrated in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: By retaining the skewness, synthetic images retained naturalistic light-dark asymmetries.
source: By retaining the skewness, these synthetic images retained naturalistic light-dark asymmetries.
evidence: This explains the rationale for including skewness.

claim: When only the mean and variance of natural scenes were retained, the third-order response was near zero and did not improve motion estimation.
source: When only the mean and variance of natural scenes were retained, the third-order response was near zero (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, green) and did not improve motion estimation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a result from the synthetic image experiments, shown in figures.

claim: When the synthetic scenes were constrained to be naturalistically light-dark asymmetric, the improvement added by the third-order kernel was recovered.
source: However, when the synthetic scenes were constrained to be naturalistically light-dark asymmetric, the improvement added by the third-order kernel was recovered (Figure 5E), with magnitude comparable to what was observed for the natural scene dataset (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the synthetic image experiments, shown in Figure 5E and compared to Figure 3C.

claim: The study generated synthetic image datasets in which the image skewness was systematically varied.
source: Finally, we wanted to see whether the degree of skewness controlled the magnitude of the improvement. We therefore generated synthetic image datasets in which we systematically varied the image skewness (Figure 5FG).
evidence: This describes additional synthetic datasets, illustrated in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: In synthetic images, the degree of skewness determined how much the third-order response could improve the full motion estimate.
source: In these synthetic images, the degree of skewness determined how much the third-order response could improve the full motion estimate (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a result from the skewness sweep, shown in Figure 5H.

claim: When the images were negatively skewed, the third-order response correlated with image velocity.
source: When the images were negatively skewed, the third-order response correlated with image velocity (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the skewness sweep, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: When images were negatively skewed, the third-order response positively correlated with the residual in the second-order response, so adding it to the second-order response decreased the model's overall performance.
source: However, since it also positively correlated with the residual in the second-order response, adding it to the second-order response decreased the model's overall performance (Figure 5—figure supplement 3CD).
evidence: This is a result from the skewness sweep, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: When the images were positively skewed, the third-order response became anticorrelated with the residual in the second-order response and thus improved the overall motion estimates.
source: When the images were positively skewed, the third-order response became anticorrelated with the residual in the second-order response and thus improved the overall motion estimates (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3CD).
evidence: This is a result from the skewness sweep, shown in figures.

claim: Positive image skewness is sufficient for the third-order signal to improve motion estimates.
source: These synthetic image sets show that positive image skewness is sufficient for the third-order signal to improve motion estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synthetic image experiments.

claim: The measured algorithm for motion estimation leverages light-dark asymmetries found in natural scenes to improve motion estimates.
source: Thus, the measured algorithm for motion estimation leverages light-dark asymmetries found in natural scenes to improve motion estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synthetic image experiments.

claim: The study first fit a Volterra series expansion to model the fly's turning behavior in response to binary stochastic stimuli, and both second- and third-order terms contributed to the turning behavior.
source: In this study, we first fit a Volterra series expansion to model the fly's turning behavior in response to binary stochastic stimuli, and both second- and third-order terms in the Volterra series contributed to the turning behavior.
evidence: This summarizes the first part of the study.

claim: The study evaluated the model's output when it was presented with an ensemble of rigidly translating natural scenes, and the second- and third-order terms combined to produce outputs that better correlated with image velocities.
source: We then evaluated the model's output when it was presented with an ensemble of rigidly translating natural scenes. There, the second- and third-order terms of the model combined to produce outputs that better correlated with image velocities.
evidence: This summarizes the second part of the study.

claim: There is no a priori reason to assume that a model fit to explain turning behavior would necessarily predict the image velocity.
source: There is no a priori reason to assume that a model fit to explain turning behavior would necessarily predict the image velocity.
evidence: This is a logical observation about the modeling approach.

claim: The results motivate the hypothesis that the magnitude of the fly's turning response is determined by an internal estimate of velocity.
source: Therefore, these results can be taken together to motivate the hypothesis that the magnitude of the fly's turning response is determined by an internal estimate of velocity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis motivated by the results.

claim: The velocity estimate is specifically tailored for natural environments, since the third-order kernel relies on light-dark asymmetries that are present in natural scenes but not in arbitrary images.
source: Furthermore, this estimate is specifically tailored for natural environments, since we found that the third-order kernel relies on light-dark asymmetries that are present in natural scenes but not in arbitrary images.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the synthetic image experiments.

claim: Skewed scenes are prevalent across natural environments.
source: Since skewed scenes are prevalent across natural environments, and many visual systems exhibit ON-OFF asymmetric visual processing (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Jin et al., 2011; Mazade et al., 2019; Pandarinath et al., 2010; Ratliff et al., 2010; Zaghloul et al., 2003), many animals are likely to use similar strategies for motion perception.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural environments.

claim: Many visual systems exhibit ON-OFF asymmetric visual processing.
source: Since skewed scenes are prevalent across natural environments, and many visual systems exhibit ON-OFF asymmetric visual processing (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Jin et al., 2011; Mazade et al., 2019; Pandarinath et al., 2010; Ratliff et al., 2010; Zaghloul et al., 2003), many animals are likely to use similar strategies for motion perception.
evidence: This is established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Many animals are likely to use similar strategies for motion perception as flies.
source: Since skewed scenes are prevalent across natural environments, and many visual systems exhibit ON-OFF asymmetric visual processing (Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Jin et al., 2011; Mazade et al., 2019; Pandarinath et al., 2010; Ratliff et al., 2010; Zaghloul et al., 2003), many animals are likely to use similar strategies for motion perception.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings and general principles.
